title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 4–5 (Night 220, continuing nights-219; the opening of the night, with its formula, stood on pages missing from the only scan of volume 2, so the text begins mid-sentence), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 220 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Its opening is lost from the only surviving scan of the second volume, and the text takes up with the king standing sword in hand, raging at the false accusation against his sons. His father-in-law King Armānūs urges him not to kill them with his own hand but to have them killed out of his sight; so the king orders his old treasurer to bind al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, carry them in chests into the wilderness, cut their throats and bring back two flasks of their blood. The treasurer takes them to a desolate place and draws his sword, and each brother begs to be killed first so as not to see the other die; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. This is the first night of the second volume of the Calcutta edition. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: مَشْهُورٌ فِي يَدِهِ وَالدَّمُ يَقْطُرُ مِنْ مَنَاخِيرِهِ مِنْ شِدَّةِ غَيْظِهِ فَسَأَلَهُ عَمَّا بِهِ
sentences.tr: mashhūrun fī yadihi wa-al-damu yaqṭuru min manākhīrihi min shiddati ghayẓihi fa-saʾalahu ʿammā bihi
sentences.l: […] drawn in his-hand, and-the-blood dripping from his-nostrils from (the) intensity (of) his-rage; and-he-asked-him about-what (was) with-him.
sentences.i: […] drawn in his hand, and blood dripping from his nostrils for the violence of his rage; and King Armānūs asked him what was the matter.
sentences.n: The beginning of this night is skipped here for now: it stood on a page missing from the only scan of this volume, and the text resumes mid-sentence. Qamar al-Zamān has drawn his sword (mashhūr, “drawn, unsheathed”), and his father-in-law King Armānūs asks what is wrong. The print has يدة and مناخيرة, misprints for يده and مناخيره, corrected here. wa-al-damu yaqṭuru, “and the blood dripping”: a circumstantial clause with wa-. manākhīr, “nostrils”, a plural beside the commoner manākhir, from mankhar, “nostril”. min shiddati ghayẓihi: min of cause, “from the violence of his rage”. ʿammā is ʿan + mā, “about what”; its shadda is printed. saʾalahu ʿammā bihi, “asked him about what was with him”: what ailed him. The ء of فسأله is printed.
sentences.gap: Opening of Night 220 (before P914L01): not in the scan

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَهُ بِجَمِيعِ مَاجَرَى مِنْ وَلَدَيْهِ الْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarahu bi-jamīʿi mā jarā min waladayhi al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi
sentences.l: And-he-informed-him of-all what-happened from his-two-sons al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad.
sentences.i: He told him all that his two sons, al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, had done.
sentences.n: The print has فاخبرة, a misprint for فاخبره, corrected here. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: the verb takes bi- for the news. The print runs mā jarā together, ماجرى, as it often does; it is kept as set. mā jarā min, “what had happened from”: what had come from his sons, that is, what (as he believes) they had done. waladayhi, “his two sons”: dual, its nūn dropped before the suffix.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ لَهُ وَهَا أَنَا دَاخِلٌ إِلَيْهِمَا لِأَقْتُلَهُمَا أَقْبَحَ قِتْلَةٍ وَأُمَثِّلَ بِهِمَا أَقْبَحَ مُثْلَةٍ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla lahu wa-hā anā dākhilun ilayhimā li-aqtulahumā aqbaḥa qitlatin wa-umaththila bihimā aqbaḥa muthlatin
sentences.l: Then he-said to-him: And-here I (am) going-in to-them-two, to-kill-them (the) foulest (of) KILLINGS, and-make-an-example of-them (the) foulest (of) EXAMPLES.
sentences.i: Then he said to him: And now I am going in to them, to put them to the foulest of deaths and make of them the foulest of examples.
sentences.n: wa-hā anā dākhilun, “and here I am, entering”: hā, “behold”, with the pronoun and an active participle, “I am this moment going in”. li-aqtulahumā: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, “in order to kill them”. qitla, on the pattern fiʿla, is “a manner of killing”, and muthla “an exemplary punishment, mutilation”; aqbaḥa qitlatin, “the foulest of killings”, is an elative standing as the verb's cognate accusative. maththala bi-, Form II, “to make an example of, mutilate”: bi- marks the victim. The shadda of وامثّل and the ḍamma of مُثلة are printed. The two halves chime: aqbaḥa qitlatin / aqbaḥa muthlatin.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ صِهْرُهُ الْمَلِكُ أَرْمَانُوسُ وَقَدِ اغْتَاظَ عَلَيْهِمَا أَيْضًا وَنِعْمَ مَا تَفْعَلُ يَا وَلَدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ṣihruhu al-maliku Armānūsu wa-qadi ightāẓa ʿalayhimā ayḍan wa-niʿma mā tafʿalu yā waladī
sentences.l: And-said to-him his-father-in-law the-king Armānūs, and-he-had-become-enraged against-them-two also: And-excellent (is) what you-do, O my-son!
sentences.i: His father-in-law, King Armānūs, who was now enraged with them too, said to him: Well done, my son!
sentences.n: ṣihr is any relative by marriage; Armānūs is the father of Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, so here “father-in-law”. wa-qadi ightāẓa, “and he had become enraged”: a circumstantial clause with wa-qad and the perfect; the kasra on qad is the helping vowel before the joining alif. ightāẓa ʿalā, Form VIII of gh-y-ẓ, “to be enraged at”. wa-niʿma mā tafʿalu, “and excellent is what you do”: niʿma, “how excellent”, with mā, “what”, as in Classical niʿimmā. The reply opens with wa-, as speech in the Nights often does. yā waladī, “my son”, the old king's fond address to his son-in-law.

sentences.t: فَلَا بَارَكَ اللَّهُ فِيهِمَا وَلَا فِي أَوْلَادٍ تَفْعَلُ هٰذِهِ الْفِعَالَ فِي حَقِّ أَبِيهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lā bāraka Allāhu fīhimā wa-lā fī awlādin tafʿalu hādhihi al-fiʿāla fī ḥaqqi abīhimā
sentences.l: So-not blessed God in-them-two, and-not in children (that) do these deeds in (the) right (of) their-father!
sentences.i: God's blessing be not on them, nor on any sons who do such deeds against their father!
sentences.n: lā bāraka Allāhu fīhimā, “may God not bless them”: lā with the perfect makes a wish, here a curse. bāraka fī, Form III, “to bless”: fī marks the one blessed. awlādin tafʿalu …, “children who do …”: a relative clause without a relative pronoun, as after an indefinite noun; the verb is feminine singular, as often with a broken plural. fī ḥaqqi abīhimā, “in regard to their father”, against him: abīhimā, “the father of the two of them”, though the clause speaks of sons in general.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ يَا وَلَدِي صَاحِبُ الْمَثَلِ يَقُولُ مَنْ لَمْ يَنْظُرْ فِى الْعَوَاقِبِ مَا الدَّهْرُ لَهُ بِصَاحِبٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin yā waladī ṣāḥibu al-mathali yaqūlu man lam yanẓur fī al-ʿawāqibi mā al-dahru lahu bi-ṣāḥibin
sentences.l: But, O my-son, (the) owner (of) the-proverb says: Who not looks into the-CONSEQUENCES, not (is) the-Time to-him a-FRIEND.
sentences.i: But, my son, as the proverb has it: He who does not look to the consequences will not have Fortune for his friend.
sentences.n: ṣāḥib al-mathal, “the owner of the proverb”: whoever first said it, the usual way of quoting a saying. man lam yanẓur … mā al-dahru lahu bi-ṣāḥibin: man, “whoever”, opens a condition, and its answer is a nominal clause denied with mā, its predicate marked with bi-, as after laysa: “Time is no friend to him”. Classical Arabic would open such an answer with fa-, fa-mā; the saying does without. naẓara fī, “to look into, consider”. dahr, “time, fortune”, the world's turning. The print spells fī with ى here, فى. The saying rhymes: al-ʿawāqib / bi-ṣāḥib.

sentences.t: وَهُمَا وَلَدَاكَ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ
sentences.tr: wa-humā waladāka ʿalā kulli ḥālin
sentences.l: And-they-two (are) your-two-sons on every state.
sentences.i: And they are your sons, whatever they have done.
sentences.n: waladāka, “your two sons”: dual nominative, its nūn dropped before the suffix. ʿalā kulli ḥālin, “in any case, whatever happens”.

sentences.t: وَيَنْبَغِي أَنْ لَا تَقْتُلَهُمَا بِيَدِكَ فَتَشْرَبَ غُصَّتَهُمَا وَتَنْدَمَ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ عَلَى قَتْلِهِمَا حَيْثُ لَا يَنْفَعُكَ النَّدَمُ
sentences.tr: wa-yanbaghī an lā taqtulahumā bi-yadika fa-tashraba ghuṣṣatahumā wa-tandama baʿda dhālika ʿalā qatlihimā ḥaythu lā yanfaʿuka al-nadamu
sentences.l: And-it-is-fitting that not you-kill-them with-your-hand, and-so-drink their-choking-grief, and-regret after that over killing-them, where not profits-you the-regret.
sentences.i: You ought not to kill them with your own hand, and then have to swallow the bitter grief of it, and afterwards repent of killing them when repentance can do you no good.
sentences.n: yanbaghī an, “it is fitting that, one ought to”: Form VII of b-gh-y. an lā, “that … not”, with the subjunctive; Classical often writes the two as one word, allā. bi-yadika: bi- of the instrument, “with your hand”. fa-tashraba, “and so drink”: fa- with the subjunctive gives what would follow. ghuṣṣa, “a choking, something stuck in the throat”, so the grief that sticks there; ghuṣṣatahumā, “the choking grief over them”; its shadda is printed. nadima ʿalā, “to regret”: ʿalā marks what is regretted. ḥaythu, “where”, here “at a time when”.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أَرْسِلْهُمَا مَعَ أَحَدٍ مِنَ الْمَمَالِيكِ لِيَقْتُلَهُمَا فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ وَهُمَا غَائِبَانِ مِنْ عَيْنَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin arsilhumā maʿa aḥadin mina al-mamālīki li-yaqtulahumā fī al-barriyyati wa-humā ghāʾibāni min ʿaynayka
sentences.l: But send-them with one of the-mamluks, so-that-he-kill-them in the-wilderness, and-they-two (being) absent from your-two-eyes.
sentences.i: Rather, send them off with one of the mamluks to kill them out in the wilderness, where they will be out of your sight.
sentences.n: arsil, Form IV imperative of r-s-l, “send”. mamālīk, plural of mamlūk, “owned”: a slave, especially a slave soldier or page. li-yaqtulahumā: li- of purpose, “that he may kill them”. barriyya, “open country, wilderness”. wa-humā ghāʾibāni, “while they are absent”: a circumstantial clause; ghāʾib, “absent”, in the dual, its ئ printed. Classical would say ghāʾib ʿan, “absent from”; the print has min.

sentences.t: كَمَا قِيلَ فِى الْمَثَلِ بُعْدِي عَنْ حَبِيبِي أَجْمَلُ وَأَحْسَنُ * عَيْنٌ لَا تَنْظُرُ وَقَلْبٌ لَا يَحْزَنُ *
sentences.tr: ka-mā qīla fī al-mathali buʿdī ʿan ḥabībī ajmalu wa-aḥsanu * ʿaynun lā tanẓuru wa-qalbun lā yaḥzanu *
sentences.l: As it-was-said in the-proverb: My-being-far from my-beloved (is) fairer and-BETTER: * an-eye (that) not looks, and-a-heart (that) not GRIEVES. *
sentences.i: As the proverb says: Better and fairer for me to be far from my beloved: * the eye that does not see, the heart that does not grieve. *
sentences.n: The print sets this saying off with stars, as it does rhymed prose. buʿdī ʿan ḥabībī, “my distance from my beloved”, is the subject, and ajmalu wa-aḥsanu, “finer and better”, the predicate: elatives without min, “better (than nearness)”. ʿaynun lā tanẓuru wa-qalbun lā yaḥzanu: two indefinite nouns, each with a relative clause, “an eye that does not look, a heart that does not grieve”: what the eye does not see, the heart does not grieve over. ʿayn is feminine, hence tanẓuru; qalb is masculine, hence yaḥzanu. The rhyme falls on aḥsan / yaḥzan.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ صِهْرِهِ الْمَلِكِ أَرْمَانُوسَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ رَآهُ صَوَابًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku Qamaru al-Zamāni min ṣihrihi al-maliki Armānūsa hādhā al-kalāma raʾāhu ṣawāban
sentences.l: And-when heard the-king Qamar al-Zamān from his-father-in-law the-king Armānūs this speech, he-saw-it right.
sentences.i: When King Qamar al-Zamān heard these words from his father-in-law, King Armānūs, he judged them right.
sentences.n: The print has صهرة, a misprint for صهره, corrected here. Armānūs is a diptote, a name that takes no tanwīn and has -a for the genitive. raʾāhu ṣawāban, “he saw it right”: raʾā takes two objects, “to consider (something) to be”. The آ of رآه is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَغْمَدَ سَيْفَهُ وَرَجَعَ وَجَلَسَ عَلَى سَرِيرِ مَمْلَكَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-aghmada sayfahu wa-rajaʿa wa-jalasa ʿalā sarīri mamlakatihi
sentences.l: And-he-sheathed his-sword, and-went-back and-sat on (the) throne (of) his-kingdom.
sentences.i: So he sheathed his sword, went back and sat down on the throne of his kingdom.
sentences.n: aghmada, Form IV of gh-m-d, “to sheathe”, from ghimd, “scabbard”.

sentences.t: وَدَعَى خَازِنْدَارَهُ وَكَانَ شَيْخًا كَبِيرًا عَارِفًا بِالْأُمُورِ وَتَقَلُّبَاتِ الدُّهُورِ
sentences.tr: wa-daʿā khāzindārahu wa-kāna shaykhan kabīran ʿārifan bi-al-umūri wa-taqallubāti al-duhūri
sentences.l: And-he-called his-treasurer, and-he-was an-old-man, great (in years), knowing in-the-AFFAIRS and-(the)-turnings (of) the-AGES.
sentences.i: And he called his treasurer, an aged man, versed in affairs and in the turns and changes of the times.
sentences.n: The print has خازندارة, a misprint for خازنداره, corrected here. daʿā, “to call, summon”, is spelled دعى, with ى where Classical writes دعا, a common spelling in the edition. khāzindār, “treasurer”, a Persian title, “keeper of the treasury”. wa-kāna shaykhan, “and he was an old man”: a circumstantial clause describing him. ʿārif bi-, “knowing, versed in”: bi- marks what is known. taqallubāt, plural of taqallub, Form V verbal noun of q-l-b, “turning about, change”; its shadda is printed. duhūr, plural of dahr, “time, fortune”. The phrase rhymes: al-umūr / al-duhūr.

sentences.t: وَ قَالَ لَهُ ادْخُلْ إِلَى وَلَدَيَّ الْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ وَكَتِّفْهُمَا كِتَافًا جَيِّدًا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu udkhul ilā waladayya al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi wa-kattifhumā kitāfan jayyidan
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Go-in to my-two-sons al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad, and-pinion-them (a) pinioning good;
sentences.i: and said to him: Go in to my two sons, al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, and tie their arms fast behind them;
sentences.n: The print sets the wa- of wa-qāla apart at the end of its line (و قال); it is kept as set. waladayya, “my two sons”: the dual ending -ay with -ya, “my”, merging as -ayya; the fatḥa and the shadda are printed, ولدَيّ. kattafa, Form II of k-t-f, from katif, “shoulder”: to tie someone's arms behind his back; its shadda is printed. kitāfan jayyidan, “a good pinioning”: kitāf, “the binding, pinioning”, as the verb's cognate accusative, “bind them well”.

sentences.t: وَاجْعَلْهُمَا فِي صُنْدُوقَيْنِ وَاحْمِلْهُمَا عَلَى بَغْلٍ وَارْكَبْ أَنْتَ وَاخْرُجْ لَهُمَا إِلَى وَسَطِ الْبَرِّيَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-ijʿalhumā fī ṣundūqayni wa-iḥmilhumā ʿalā baghlin wa-irkab anta wa-ukhruj lahumā ilā wasaṭi al-barriyyati
sentences.l: and-put-them-two in two-chests, and-load-them on a-mule, and-ride, you, and-go-out for-them to (the) middle (of) the-wilderness;
sentences.i: put them in two chests, load them on a mule, mount yourself, and take them out into the heart of the wilderness;
sentences.n: jaʿala fī, “to put into”. ṣundūq, “chest, box”; ṣundūqayni, dual genitive. irkab anta, “ride, you”: the pronoun points the contrast, the princes going on the mule and the treasurer riding. ukhruj lahumā, “go out for them”: one would expect bihimā, “with them”, as the narrative has a little later (kharaja bihimā); li- is odd here, and the sense is “take them out”. The shadda of البرّية is printed.

sentences.t: وَاذْبَحْهُمَا وَامْلَأْ لِي قَنَانِيَتَيْنِ مِنْ دَمِهِمَا وَائْتِنِي بِهِمَا عَاجِلًا
sentences.tr: wa-idhbaḥhumā wa-imlaʾ lī qanāniyatayni min damihimā wa-iʾtinī bihimā ʿājilan
sentences.l: and-slaughter-them, and-fill for-me two-flasks from their-blood, and-come-to-me with-them quickly.
sentences.i: there cut their throats, and fill me two flasks with their blood, and bring them to me at once.
sentences.n: dhabaḥa, “to slaughter, cut the throat”, the word for killing a beast. The hamza of imlaʾ, “fill”, and of iʾtinī, “come to me”, is printed: واملأ, وائتني. qanāniyatayni, “two flasks”: the print's قنانيتين is the dual of qanāniya, a later form not found in the classical lexica, where a flask is qinnīna (plural qanānī); the meaning is not in doubt. lī, “for me”: li- of benefit. atā bi-, “to come with”, is “to bring”: iʾtinī bihimā, “bring them to me”, the two flasks. ʿājilan, “quickly”, an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَازِنْدَارُ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khāzindāru samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-treasurer: Hearing and-obedience.
sentences.i: The treasurer said to him: With hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”: two accusatives with their verb understood, the servant's formula of consent.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَهَضَ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الْأَمْجَدِ وَالْأَسْعَدِ فَصَادَفَهُمَا فِى الطَّرِيقِ وَهُمَا خَارِجَانِ مِنْ دِهْلِيزِ الْقَصْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma nahaḍa min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-tawajjaha ilā al-Amjadi wa-al-Asʿadi fa-ṣādafahumā fī al-ṭarīqi wa-humā khārijāni min dihlīzi al-qaṣri
sentences.l: Then he-rose from his-time and-his-hour, and-made-his-way to al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad, and-came-upon-them in the-way, and-they-two (were) coming-out from (the) vestibule (of) the-palace.
sentences.i: Then he rose that very moment and went to find al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, and he came upon them on the way as they were coming out of the palace vestibule.
sentences.n: min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”: at once, that very moment. tawajjaha ilā, Form V, “to turn towards, make for”; its shadda is printed. ṣādafa, Form III, “to come upon, meet by chance”. wa-humā khārijāni, “while they were coming out”: a circumstantial clause, with the dual active participle. dihlīz, a Persian loanword, “entrance hall, vestibule”.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ لَبِسَا قُمَاشَهُمَا وَأَفْخَرَ ثِيَابِهِمَا وَأَرَادَا التَّوَجُّهَ إِلَى وَالِدِهِمَا الْمَلِكِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ لِيُسَلِّمَا عَلَيْهِ وَيُهَنِّيَاهُ بِالسَّلَامَةِ عِنْدَ قُدُومِهِ مِنَ السَّفَرِ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad labisā qumāshahumā wa-afkhara thiyābihimā wa-arādā al-tawajjuha ilā wālidihimā al-maliki Qamari al-Zamāni li-yusallimā ʿalayhi wa-yuhanniyāhu bi-al-salāmati ʿinda qudūmihi mina al-safari ilā al-ṣaydi
sentences.l: And-they-two-had put-on their-stuff and-(the)-finest (of) their-clothes, and-wanted the-going to their-father the-king Qamar al-Zamān, so-that-they-greet him and-congratulate-him on-the-safety at his-arrival from the-journey to the-hunt.
sentences.i: They had put on their finery, the most splendid clothes they had, and were about to go to their father, King Qamar al-Zamān, to greet him and wish him joy of his safe return from his hunting trip.
sentences.n: wa-qad labisā, “they had put on”: wa-qad with the perfect, a circumstance already complete. qumāsh, “stuff, cloth”, here their good clothes; afkhara thiyābihimā, “the finest of their clothes”, an elative in iḍāfa. li-yusallimā: li- of purpose with the subjunctive, dual, its nūn dropped. sallama ʿalā, Form II, “to greet”; its shadda is printed, as is the shadda of ويهنّياه. yuhanniyāhu, “that they congratulate him”: from hannaʾa, Form II, with its hamza turned into yāʾ, a common later spelling, where Classical would write يهنّئاه. After hannaʾa, bi- marks the occasion: bi-al-salāmati, “on his safe return”. al-safar ilā al-ṣayd, “the journey to the hunt”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُمَا الْخَازِنْدَارُ قَبَضَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَقَالَ لَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhumā al-khāzindāru qabaḍa ʿalayhimā wa-qāla lahumā
sentences.l: And-when saw-them-two the-treasurer, he-seized upon-them-two and-said to-them-two:
sentences.i: When the treasurer saw them, he laid hold of them and said to them:
sentences.n: qabaḍa ʿalā, “to seize, lay hold of”: ʿalā marks the one seized. The آ of رآهما is printed.

sentences.t: يَا وَلَدَايَ اعْلَمَا أَنَّنِي عَبْدٌ مَأْمُورٌ وَأَنَّ أَبَاكُمَا قَدْ أَمَرَنِي بِأَمْرٍ فَهَلْ أَنْتُمَا طَائِعَانِ لِأَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: yā waladāya iʿlamā annanī ʿabdun maʾmūrun wa-anna abākumā qad amaranī bi-amrin fa-hal antumā ṭāʾiʿāni li-amrihi
sentences.l: O my-two-sons, know-you-two that-I (am) a-slave commanded, and-that your-father has ordered-me with-an-order; so-are you-two obedient to-his-order?
sentences.i: My sons, know that I am a slave and must do as I am bidden, and your father has given me an order: will you submit to his command?
sentences.n: The print has لامرة, a misprint for لامره, corrected here. yā waladāya, “O my two sons”: the dual keeps its nominative -ā before -ya, “my”, where Classical Arabic has yā waladayya; the later language often does so. ʿabd maʾmūr, “a slave under orders”: maʾmūr, passive participle of amara, “commanded”. amara bi-, “to order”: bi- marks the thing ordered, bi-amrin, “with an order”. ṭāʾiʿ li-, “obedient to”: li- marks what is obeyed; the ئ of طائعان is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qālā naʿam
sentences.l: They-two-said: Yes.
sentences.i: They said: Yes.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِمَا الْخَازِنْدَارُ وَ كَتَّفَهُمَا وَوَضَعَهُمَا فِي صُنْدُوقَيْنِ وَحَمَلَهُمَا عَلَى ظَهْرِ بَغْلٍ وَخَرَجَ بِهِمَا مِنَ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika taqaddama ilayhimā al-khāzindāru wa-kattafahumā wa-waḍaʿahumā fī ṣundūqayni wa-ḥamalahumā ʿalā ẓahri baghlin wa-kharaja bihimā mina al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-at that stepped-up to-them-two the-treasurer, and-pinioned-them, and-put-them in two-chests, and-loaded-them on (the) back (of) a-mule, and-went-out with-them from the-city.
sentences.i: Thereupon the treasurer stepped up to them, bound their arms, put them in two chests, loaded them on a mule's back and took them out of the city.
sentences.n: ʿinda dhālika, “at that”, thereupon. taqaddama ilā, Form V, “to step up to”; its shadda is printed, as is that of كتّفهما. Again the print sets a wa- apart at the end of its line, before kattafahumā (و كتّفهما); it is kept as set. kharaja bi-, “to go out with”, to take out: bi- of accompaniment.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ يَزَلْ سَائِرًا بِهِمَا فِى الْبَرِّيَّةِ إِلَى قَرِيبِ الظُّهْرِ فَأَنْزَلَهُمَا فِي مَكَانٍ قَفْرٍ مُوحِشٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lam yazal sāʾiran bihimā fī al-barriyyati ilā qarībi al-ẓuhri fa-anzalahumā fī makānin qafrin mūḥishin
sentences.l: And-not he-ceased going with-them in the-wilderness until near the-noon, and-he-set-them-down in a-place empty, desolate.
sentences.i: He went on and on with them through the wilderness until close on noon, and then he set them down in a barren, desolate spot.
sentences.n: lam yazal sāʾiran, “he did not cease going”: lam yazal with an accusative participle, “he kept on going”; the ئ of سائرا is printed. sāra bi-, “to go with”, to carry along. ilā qarībi al-ẓuhri, “until near noon”: ẓuhr, midday, the time of the noon prayer. anzala, Form IV, “to bring down, set down”. qafr, “empty, waterless land”, here used as an adjective; mūḥish, Form IV participle of w-ḥ-sh, “desolate, fearsome”.

sentences.t: وَنَزَلَ عَنْ فَرَسِهِ وَحَطَّ الصُّنْدُوقَيْنِ عَنْ ظَهْرِ الْبَغْلِ وَفَتَحَهُمَا وَأَخْرَجَ الْأَمْجَدَ وَالْأَسْعَدَ مِنْهُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-nazala ʿan farasihi wa-ḥaṭṭa al-ṣundūqayni ʿan ẓahri al-baghli wa-fataḥahumā wa-akhraja al-Amjada wa-al-Asʿada minhumā
sentences.l: And-he-came-down from his-horse, and-put-down the-two-chests from (the) back (of) the-mule, and-opened-them, and-brought-out al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad from-them.
sentences.i: He got down from his horse, lifted the two chests off the mule's back, opened them and took al-Amjad and al-Asʿad out.
sentences.n: nazala ʿan, “to get down from”. ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, lower”; its shadda is printed. al-ṣundūqayni, dual accusative.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا نَظَرَ إِلَيْهِمَا بَكَى بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا عَلَى حُسْنِهِمَا وَجَمَالِهِمَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā naẓara ilayhimā bakā bukāʾan shadīdan ʿalā ḥusnihimā wa-jamālihimā
sentences.l: And-when he-looked at-them-two, he-wept a-weeping severe over their-beauty and-their-loveliness.
sentences.i: When he looked at them, he wept bitterly over their beauty and grace.
sentences.n: bakā bukāʾan shadīdan, “he wept a severe weeping”: the verbal noun as cognate object with an adjective, “he wept bitterly”; the ء of بكاء is printed. bakā ʿalā, “to weep over”. ḥusn and jamāl, “beauty” and “loveliness”, a near-synonym pair.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ جَرَّدَ سَيْفَهُ وَقَالَ لَهُمَا وَاللَّهِ يَاسَيِّدَايَ إِنَّهُ يَعِزُّ عَلَيَّ أَنْ أَفْعَلَ بِكُمَا فِعْلًا قَبِيحًا
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika jarrada sayfahu wa-qāla lahumā wa-Allāhi yā sayyidāya innahu yaʿizzu ʿalayya an afʿala bikumā fiʿlan qabīḥan
sentences.l: And-after that he-bared his-sword, and-said to-them-two: By-God, O-my-two-masters, indeed-it is-hard upon-me that I-do to-you-two a-deed foul;
sentences.i: After that he drew his sword and said to them: By God, my masters, it grieves me to do so foul a thing to you;
sentences.n: jarrada, Form II, “to bare, unsheathe”; its shadda is printed. yā sayyidāya, “O my two masters”, run together in the print, ياسيداي: like yā waladāya above, the dual keeps its -ā before -ya. innahu yaʿizzu ʿalayya an …, “it is hard upon me that …”: -hu is the pronoun of the matter, “it is the case that”; ʿazza ʿalā, “to be grievous to”. The shaddas of يعزّ and عليّ are printed. faʿala bi-, “to do to”: bi- marks the one it is done to.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ أَنَا مَعْذُورٌ فِي هٰذِهِ الْأُمُورِ لِأَنَّنِي عَبْدٌ مَأْمُورٌ وَقَدْ أَمَرَنِي وَالِدُكُمَا الْمَلِكُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ بِضَرْبِ رِقَابِكُمَا
sentences.tr: wa-lākin anā maʿdhūrun fī hādhihi al-umūri li-annanī ʿabdun maʾmūrun wa-qad amaranī wālidukumā al-maliku Qamaru al-Zamāni bi-ḍarbi riqābikumā
sentences.l: but I (am) excused in these MATTERS, because-I (am) a-slave COMMANDED, and-has ordered-me your-father the-king Qamar al-Zamān with (the) striking (of) your-necks.
sentences.i: but I am not to blame in this, for I am a slave and must obey; and your father, King Qamar al-Zamān, has ordered me to strike off your heads.
sentences.n: wa-lākin anā: lākin, the light form of “but”, followed by a pronoun as subject. maʿdhūr, “excused”, passive participle of ʿadhara. li-annanī, “because I”: li-, “for”, with anna. The clause rhymes: al-umūr / maʾmūr. amara bi-, “to order”: bi- marks the thing ordered, bi-ḍarbi riqābikumā, “the striking of your necks”, beheading; riqāb, plural of raqaba, “neck”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لَهُ أَيُّهَا الْأَمِيرُ افْعَلْ مَاأَمَرَكَ بِهِ الْمَلِكُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā lahu ayyuhā al-amīru ifʿal mā amaraka bihi al-maliku
sentences.l: And-they-two-said to-him: O the-emir, do what-ordered-you with-it the-king.
sentences.i: They said to him: Emir, do what the king has commanded you.
sentences.n: ayyuhā al-amīru, “O emir”: a courtesy title for the old treasurer; the shadda of ايّها is printed. mā amaraka bihi, run together in the print as ماامرك: “what he ordered you with it”, the bi- of amara bi-, with -hi going back to mā.

sentences.t: فَنَحْنُ صَابِرُونَ عَلَى مَا قَدَّرَهُ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ عَلَيْنَا وَأَنْتَ فِي حِلٍّ مِنْ دِمَائِنَا
sentences.tr: fa-naḥnu ṣābirūna ʿalā mā qaddarahu Allāhu ʿazza wa-jalla ʿalaynā wa-anta fī ḥillin min dimāʾinā
sentences.l: For-we (are) bearing-patiently over what decreed-it God, (He is) mighty and-(He is)-majestic, upon-us; and-you (are) in release from our-bloods.
sentences.i: We bear with patience what God, mighty and majestic, has decreed for us, and you are free of any guilt for our blood.
sentences.n: The print has قدّرة, a misprint for قدّره, corrected here. ṣabara ʿalā, “to bear patiently”: ṣābirūna is the plural participle, where the two of them might use the dual. qaddara ʿalā, Form II, “to decree for, ordain upon”. ʿazza wa-jalla, “mighty is He and majestic”, the pious formula after God's name. The shaddas of قدّره, عزّ, جلّ and حلّ are printed. fī ḥillin min dimāʾinā, “in release from our blood”: absolved of it, a formula by which the victim forgives the killer. dimāʾ, plural of dam, “blood”; its ئ is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا تَعَانَقَا وَوَدَّعَا بَعْضَهُمَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā taʿānaqā wa-waddaʿā baʿḍahumā
sentences.l: Then indeed-they-two embraced-each-other, and-bade-farewell-to some-of-them.
sentences.i: Then they embraced and bade each other farewell.
sentences.n: taʿānaqā, Form VI of ʿ-n-q, from ʿunuq, “neck”: “they embraced each other”. waddaʿa, Form II, “to bid farewell”; its shadda is printed. baʿḍahumā, “some of them”, used as “each other”, a later reciprocal where Classical says baʿḍuhumā baʿḍan.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ لِلْخَازِنْدَارِ بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ يَاعَمِّ إِنَّكَ لَاتُجَزِّعْنِي غُصَّةَ أَخِي وَلَا تَسْقِنِي حَسْرَتَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-Asʿadu li-al-khāzindāri bi-Allāhi ʿalayka yā ʿammi innaka lā tujazziʿnī ghuṣṣata akhī wa-lā tasqinī ḥasratahu
sentences.l: And-said al-Asʿad to-the-treasurer: By-God upon-you, O-uncle, indeed-you, (do) not make-me-grieve (the) choking (for) my-brother, and-(do)-not give-me-to-drink his-anguish;
sentences.i: And al-Asʿad said to the treasurer: For God's sake, uncle, do not make me suffer the bitter grief of my brother's death, nor give me the anguish of it to drink;
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God upon you”: I adjure you by God. yā ʿammi, “O uncle”, run together as ياعم: ʿamm, “paternal uncle”, the polite address to an older man; the -ī of “my” falls away in the vocative. innaka lā tujazziʿnī … wa-lā tasqinī: after innaka, “indeed you”, come two prohibitions with lā and the jussive; tasqinī, from saqā, “to give to drink”, has lost its final yāʾ, so it is jussive, and tujazziʿnī is read the same way. The print runs lā tujazziʿnī together as لاتجزعني. jazzaʿa, Form II of j-z-ʿ, “to make (someone) grieve, distress”, here with ghuṣṣata akhī as a second object. One might expect lā tujarriʿnī, “do not make me swallow”, from jarraʿa, which goes naturally with ghuṣṣa, “a choking draught”, and with tasqinī after it; ز and ر differ by a single dot, but جزّع also gives a sense, and the print is kept. ḥasra, “grief, anguish”.

sentences.t: بَلِ اقْتُلْنِي أَنَا قَبْلَهُ لِيَكُونَ ذٰلِكَ أَهْوَنَ عَلَيَّ
sentences.tr: bali uqtulnī anā qablahu li-yakūna dhālika ahwana ʿalayya
sentences.l: rather, kill-me, me, before-him, so-that be that easier upon-me.
sentences.i: no, kill me first, before him, so that it may go easier with me.
sentences.n: bali, “rather”, with the helping kasra before the joining alif. uqtulnī anā, “kill me, me”: the independent pronoun repeats the object suffix for emphasis. li-yakūna: li- of purpose with the subjunctive. ahwan, “easier, lighter”, elative of hayyin; ʿalayya, “upon me”, its shadda printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ لِلْخَازِنْدَارِ مِثْلَ مَاقَالَ الْأَسْعَدُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla al-Amjadu li-al-khāzindāri mithla mā qāla al-Asʿadu
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad to-the-treasurer (the) like (of) what-said al-Asʿad.
sentences.i: And al-Amjad said the same to the treasurer as al-Asʿad had said.
sentences.n: mithla mā qāla, “the like of what he said”, mā qāla run together in the print as ماقال. mithla is the object of qāla.

sentences.t: وَاسْتَعْطَفَ الْخَازِنْدَارَ أَنْ يَقْتُلَهُ قَبْلَ أَخِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-istaʿṭafa al-khāzindāra an yaqtulahu qabla akhīhi
sentences.l: And-he-sought-the-pity-of the-treasurer that he-kill-him before his-brother.
sentences.i: He begged the treasurer to have pity and kill him before his brother.
sentences.n: istaʿṭafa, Form X of ʿ-ṭ-f, “to seek someone's sympathy, entreat”, takes the person as its object and the request in a clause with an.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ إِنَّ أَخِي أَصْغَرُ مِنِّي فَلَا تُذِقْنِي لَوْعَتَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu inna akhī aṣgharu minnī fa-lā tudhiqnī lawʿatahu
sentences.l: And-he-said to-him: Indeed my-brother (is) younger than-me, so-(do)-not make-me-taste his-burning-grief.
sentences.i: And he said to him: My brother is younger than I am, so do not make me taste the pain of losing him.
sentences.n: aṣgharu minnī, “younger than me”: an elative with min. adhāqa, Form IV of dh-w-q, “to make taste”, takes two objects; tudhiqnī is jussive after the prohibitive lā. lawʿa, “the burning pain of love or grief”; lawʿatahu, “the anguish for him”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى كُلٌّ مِنْهُمَا بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ وَبَكَى الْخَازِنْدَارُ لِبُكَائِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma bakā kullun minhumā bukāʾan shadīdan mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin wa-bakā al-khāzindāru li-bukāʾihimā
sentences.l: Then wept each of-them-two a-weeping severe, not upon-it of increase; and-wept the-treasurer at-their-weeping.
sentences.i: Then each of them wept so bitterly that none could weep more, and the treasurer wept to see them weep.
sentences.n: mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin, “there is no increase upon it”: nothing could exceed it, a stock phrase of the Nights. li-bukāʾihimā: li- of cause, “at their weeping”. The ء of بكاء and the ئ of لبكائهما are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
